content: A burette, also known as a buret, is a vertical cylindrical piece of laboratory glassware. It is equipped with volumetric graduations along its entire length and features a precision tap or stopcock at its bottom. This apparatus is specifically designed to dispense precise amounts of liquid reagents, which is essential in experiments requiring high accuracy, such as titration experiments. When using a burette, its precision necessitates careful handling to avoid systematic errors. To ensure accurate readings, the observer's eyes must be level with the graduation marks to prevent parallax errors. The thickness of the printed lines on the burette is also significant; the bottom of the liquid meniscus should align with the top of the desired graduation line for accurate measurement. If the bottom of the meniscus aligns with the bottom of the line, the measurement may deviate by approximately 0.02 mL. Due to the high precision of the burette, even a single drop of liquid hanging from its tip must be transferred to the receiving flask. This is typically achieved by touching the drop to the side of the receiving flask and rinsing it into the solution using the experimental solvent, which is often water. By carefully controlling the stopcock and rinsing, even partial drops of liquid can be added to the receiving flask with precision. The history of the burette is closely tied to the development of volumetric analysis. François Antoine Henri Descroizilles created the first burette in 1791, which resembled a graduated cylinder. Later, in 1824, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac improved the design by adding a side arm and introduced the terms pipette and burette in a paper on the standardization of indigo solutions. A significant advancement in the methodology and widespread adoption of volumetric analysis was achieved by Karl Friedrich Mohr, who redesigned the burette by incorporating a clamp and a tip at its bottom.
